# Problem 1
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(broom)

homicide_raw <- read_csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/washingtonpost/data-homicides/master/homicide-data.csv"
)

homicide_df <- homicide_raw |>
  mutate(
    city_state  = str_c(city, ", ", state),
    solved      = as.integer(disposition == "Closed by arrest"),   # 1 = solved, 0 = not
    victim_race = str_to_lower(victim_race),
    victim_age  = as.numeric(victim_age)                           # "Unknown" -> NA (warning is expected)
  ) |>
  filter(
    !city_state %in% c("Dallas, TX", "Phoenix, AZ", "Kansas City, MO", "Tulsa, AL"),
    victim_race %in% c("white", "black"),
    victim_sex  %in% c("Male", "Female")        # drop "Unknown" sex so male vs female is well defined
  ) |>
  mutate(
    victim_race = factor(victim_race, levels = c("white", "black")),   # white = reference
    victim_sex  = factor(victim_sex,  levels = c("Female", "Male"))    # female = reference
  )

baltimore_df <- homicide_df |> filter(city_state == "Baltimore, MD")

baltimore_fit <- glm(
  solved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race,
  data = baltimore_df, family = binomial()
)

baltimore_fit |>
  tidy(conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |>
  select(term, OR = estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

city_results <- homicide_df |>
  nest(data = -city_state) |>
  mutate(
    fit  = map(data, possibly(
      \(d) glm(solved ~ victim_age + victim_sex + victim_race, data = d, family = binomial()),
      otherwise = NULL)),
    tidy = map(fit, \(m) if (is.null(m)) NULL else tidy(m, conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE))
  ) |>
  select(city_state, tidy) |>
  unnest(tidy) |>
  filter(term == "victim_sexMale") |>
  select(city_state, OR = estimate, conf.low, conf.high)

city_results |>
  mutate(city_state = fct_reorder(city_state, OR)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = OR, y = city_state)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Adjusted OR of a solved homicide: male vs. female victims",
    x = "Adjusted odds ratio (95% CI)", y = NULL
  )
```

The plot shows the adjusted odds ratio of a solved homicide for male vs. female victims in each city . Most cities have an estimated OR below 1, so cases with male victims are less likely to be solved than those with female victims. In roughly the lower half of the plot, the confidence intervals lie entirely below 1, indicating a clear difference. In the upper part, the intervals cross 1, so the data are consistent with no difference. Only Albuquerque, Stockton, and Fresno have point estimates above 1, and their wide intervals include 1. Wide intervals reflect cities with few homicides, so those estimates are imprecise.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(modelr)
library(broom)
library(p8105.datasets)

data("weather_df")

set.seed(1)

boot_df <- weather_df |>
  drop_na(tmax, tmin, prcp) |>
  bootstrap(n = 5000) |>
  mutate(
    models = map(strap, \(s) lm(tmax ~ tmin + prcp, data = s)),
    r2     = map_dbl(models, \(m) glance(m)$r.squared),
    beta1  = map_dbl(models, \(m) coef(m)[["tmin"]]),
    beta2  = map_dbl(models, \(m) coef(m)[["prcp"]]),
    ratio  = beta1 / beta2
  )

# ---- Distributions ----
boot_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = r2)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  labs(title = "Bootstrap distribution of r-squared", x = "r-squared")

boot_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = ratio)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60) +
  labs(title = "Bootstrap distribution of beta1 / beta2", x = "beta1 / beta2")

# ---- 95% bootstrap percentile CIs ----
boot_df |>
  summarize(
    r2_lower    = quantile(r2, 0.025),
    r2_upper    = quantile(r2, 0.975),
    ratio_lower = quantile(ratio, 0.025),
    ratio_upper = quantile(ratio, 0.975)
  )
```
The bootstrap distribution of r̂² is unimodal and roughly symmetric, centered at about 0.941, with a slightly longer left tail. The estimates are tightly concentrated, with almost all values between about 0.93 and 0.95, so the model’s fit is very stable across bootstrap samples. The 95% bootstrap CI is roughly 0.935 to 0.947.

The distribution of the ratio of the tmin coefficient to the prcp coefficient is unimodal and left-skewed, with a peak around −175 and a long tail toward more negative values. Every bootstrap estimate is negative, because the tmin coefficient is positive and the prcp coefficient is negative in all samples. The spread is large compared with the typical value, because the prcp coefficient is small and dividing by it amplifies sampling variability. The 95% bootstrap CI is roughly −270 to −130, so the ratio is estimated much less precisely than r̂²
